stem: Which combination of features is most supportive of central hypotonia in a floppy infant?

options.text: Impaired alertness, seizures, poor feeding or sucking, and dysmorphic features
Curled toes when bearing weight and a positive fog manoeuvre
Asymmetric hopping with difficulty heel walking
Gower's sign with difficulty rising from a low chair
Head lag alone without any other features

explanation: Central hypotonia is most supported by associated central neurological and dysmorphic features. Impaired alertness, seizures, poor feeding or sucking, and dysmorphic features fit this pattern best.

citations.source: Louisa Leone MD3 2025 - Child and Adolescent Health - Study Notes.pdf
citations.title: Louisa Leone MD3 2025 - Child and Adolescent Health - Study Notes.pdf

optionExplanations.A: Correct because impaired alertness, seizures, poor feeding or sucking, and dysmorphic features are classic associated features of central hypotonia.
optionExplanations.B: Incorrect because curled toes on weight bearing and a positive fog manoeuvre are examination signs of spasticity, not the central hypotonia feature cluster.
optionExplanations.C: Incorrect because asymmetric hopping and difficulty heel walking are gait findings, not features that support central hypotonia in a floppy infant.
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect because Gower's sign and difficulty rising from a low chair suggest proximal muscle weakness, not central hypotonia.
optionExplanations.E: Incorrect because head lag alone is non-specific and is not as supportive of central hypotonia as a cluster of associated central features.
